synopsis: Field exposure alone cannot demonstrate rare-event safety, including for off-road machines; the proposed alternative combines stratified testing, simulation and safety analysis, while the required field exposure for rare misses or unintended braking remains uncertain [f312, f6924, f5467, f8181]. The sampling burden is substantial: zero observed misses requires 299 independent trials to demonstrate a miss rate of at most 1%, or 29,956 for at most 0.01%, and RAND’s on-road estimate reaches hundreds of millions of miles [f13303, f13304, f13305]. In 2016, Michigan researchers reported importance-sampling acceleration factors of roughly 300–100,000 for car-following crashes and 2,000–20,000 for lane-change conflicts, but credible rare-event estimates require valid input distributions and tail models, and the glossary identifies no known exposure distribution for 100 or more site types [f1220, f1221, f8183, f11614]. Simulation can deliberately generate rare events and corner cases, but only for conceived and parameterised hazards; procedural scenes can miss real correlations and rare structures, while design-of-experiments methods cannot establish global corner-case coverage or exclude narrow nonlinear failures [f13307, f3793, f7215, f7222]. Selected difficult cases therefore warrant qualification-quality sensor models and higher-fidelity machine models where simpler models fail, followed by controlled whole-machine confirmation of worst cases [f4474, f6409, f719]. The recommended pilot is a difficult end-to-end slice with physical or bench comparators and predeclared decision criteria, using 3–5 scenario classes including at least one edge case; a four-month window cannot cover all seasons, rare events or operator adaptation [f9914, f9916, f12348].
